Imagine the switch that ends your growth never flips.
Twenty-five centimetres every year, and it never slows.
You are standing on the square of an old Dutch town.
Today you stand one point eight metres tall.
Sixty years of that adds fifteen metres.
You notice it in your shoes first.
Every pair splits within the year.
People stop, move back, and look up at you.
Their heads come up to your knee.
In year four you passed the tallest person in history.
He reached two point seven two metres, one hundred and ninety-nine kilos.
The town is too small now, so you walk through the houses.
The last people leave, and the roofs break at your hip.
Every part of you grows together, so at the end you weigh eight hundred times more.
But your bones end up only eighty-seven times stronger.
You stand over the whole town at sixteen point eight metres.
The windmill comes up to your chest, the roofs to your thigh.
You lie down across the canal like a bridge.
Rowing boats drift under your arm.
Nothing that lived was built to be this long.
And sixty years were only the beginning.
